body.text: On November 19, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will deliver its judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar case, concerning Myanmar’s alleged violations of the Genocide Convention against the Rohingya. For our community, this is not simply another consequential moment in international law but is rather the culmination of decades of persecution and nearly 10 years of waiting for accountability. During that time, we have struggled to have the world acknowledge what we have known through lived experience: that we have endured a campaign of destruction because of who we are.
I was in the courtroom at the ICJ for the opening session of the case in 2019. I felt then, as I have felt throughout my own lived experience, how much justice and truth-telling matter.
Yet as the judgment approaches, the conversation is being pulled away from the people whose lives are at stake.

In September, a Wall Street Journal opinion piece by Orde F. Kittrie and Andres B. Munoz-Mosquera warned that the ICJ could lower the legal threshold for genocide, with implications for South Africa’s case against Israel and potential claims against the United States and NATO members. It suggested that the Trump administration could sanction judges who voted to lower the threshold. In October, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz amplified the argument, invoking Washington’s sanctions against the International Criminal Court. What happens to the independence of international justice when powerful states threaten consequences for judicial interpretations they find inconvenient?

Professor Michael Becker, a former ICJ legal officer, explained in a recent lecture that the Court’s treatment of genocidal intent could have repercussions for South Africa’s case. Both raise questions about how intent can be inferred from patterns of conduct when states invoke military or counterterrorism operations.

That is a legitimate legal discussion. But the possibility that a judgment on the Rohingya could affect another state is not a reason to politically contain our case. As Professor John Packer of the University of Ottawa has reminded us, there is no separate or adjustable genocide threshold to be lowered according to whose interests are affected. The law is the Genocide Convention, and the question is whether the evidence satisfies it. The law cannot be universal in principle but selectively protected in practice.
And yet, in all this discussion, I find myself asking a more fundamental question: where are the Rohingya?

Where are the women and girls who survived the 2017 campaign, the families who watched their homes disappear, the children who have spent nearly a decade in refugee camps without citizenship or a prospect of going home?

Human Rights Watch’s 2017 report, “All of My Body Was Pain,” documented the experiences of 52 Rohingya women and girls, including 29 survivors of rape. Their accounts described sexual violence committed alongside killings, the destruction of villages, and forced displacement. Those women carried their trauma across the Naf River into the camps, without adequate healthcare, justice, or the security of knowing they will not be forced to flee again.

The world has become comfortable discussing the Rohingya as a legal question, a humanitarian issue, or a diplomatic inconvenience. But there are human beings behind every one of these descriptions: women living with the consequences of sexual violence, children whose futures have been shaped by crimes they did not commit, families waiting for a country that will recognize them as citizens.
A judgment cannot return a murdered child to a mother or give back the years stolen from a generation. But recognition matters. Accountability matters. Being heard matters.

Some legal commentators see The Gambia v. Myanmar as a stepping stone for other proceedings. For the Rohingya it is our case, the product of years of organizing, survivor testimony, and advocacy. We did not spend decades fighting erasure so that our suffering could become a footnote in somebody else’s legal argument. Do the Rohingya not deserve justice in our own right? Must our suffering first prove useful to another cause before it is worthy of attention?

Governments invoke the catchcry of “Never Again” while humanitarian resources shrink. Permanent refugee settlements are not a solution, and detention centers offer no protection. A world that debates whether genocide can be legally established while withdrawing the resources to protect its survivors is failing the people the Convention was created to protect.

For the Rohingya, November 19 will not mark the end of our struggle, whatever the Court decides. A finding against Myanmar would be a historic step. But it would not return us home, restore our citizenship, recognize our identity, or dismantle the systems that made genocide possible. That requires sustained international pressure and a credible process of transitional justice. And if the Court does not find Myanmar responsible, that judgment will not erase documented atrocities, invalidate survivor testimony, or end our pursuit of justice.

Rohingya-led universal jurisdiction initiatives, including the genocide case in Indonesia I have pursued as a lead complainant represented by Themis Indonesia, and supported by the Myanmar Accountability Project, show that our community is not waiting passively for one institution to decide its future. We have been building alternative pathways to justice.

But first, the judges must be allowed to do their work. Their responsibility is to assess the evidence and apply the law, not to reassure Washington or preempt the consequences of a judgment for another conflict.
There will be other cases and other judgments. But for the Rohingya, this moment has been nearly a decade in the making.

Let the evidence speak and the law be applied without political intimidation. And let the Rohingya have this moment without being subordinated to somebody else’s geopolitical anxieties. We will live with the consequences of this judgment long after the commentators have moved on to their next debate.
